newsitem.title: UK: Iraqi oil said imminent but is anyone ready to buy?.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi oil said imminent but is anyone ready to buy?.

text.p: Despite the apparently imminent return of Iraqi oil exports, not one oil company admitted to signing a supply contract nor had any hired a ship to carry Iraqi oil, tanker brokers said on Monday.
Though Baghdad said it would resume oil exports on Tuesday, traders and shipping sources said it was highly unlikely Iraqi oil would hit the market for at least a couple of weeks, at the soonest.
Spokesmen for France's Elf Aquitaine and Total, two of the first companies expected to be awarded contracts, said on Monday their firms had not signed deals yet.
"We have not signed anything yet," the Elf spokesman said.
The Total spokesman said his company "in principle" is expected to buy 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) but had not finalised the agreement.

Five of the world's leading tanker brokerages told Reuters that no company has even expressed interest in hiring tankers to load crude at the Middle East Gulf port of Mina al Bakr or Turkey's Ceyhan, linked by pipeline to Iraqi oil centre Kirkuk.
"There has been not one call from companies seeking loading dates, rates or anything from the Iraqi export outlets," a London tanker broker said.

Barring last minute obstacles, United Nations Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Monday is expected to give the go-ahead to implement an oil-for-food plan allowing Baghdad to sell crude for the first time since August 1990 when it invaded Kuwait.
Iraqi newspapers on Monday were filled with reports that Iraqi oil would flow on Tuesday at 0500 GMT.
But the tanker market was more sceptical.
"If no one has even put out an enquiry for a ship, it is difficult to see that oil getting to the market for a while," one broker said.
Former Iraqi Oil Minister Issam Al-Chalabi, now an industry consultant in Amman, Jordan, doubted whether Iraqi oil exports would resume this month given the various possible logistical problems.

"There is a distinction between pumping and exporting crude...The (companies) who went (to Baghdad) are not signing contracts but confirming an interest, putting final touches and waiting for another round," Chalabi said.
He said Turkish oil company Tupras was likely to be the first to buy Iraqi oil since the first barrels will flow to Ceyhan.

"I think the Iraqis have been a bit too optimistic in expecting to ship on Tuesday. Not one contract has been signed yet. Probably Turkey will be the only ones taking the Iraqi oil as early as Tuesday," said Oystein Berentsen, head of international crude oil trading at Norwegian oil company Statoil .
If only Turkey takes the oil, storage facilities at Ceyhan will soon be filled, industry sources said.

An official from Turkey's state pipeline company Botas said storage tanks at Ceyhan were about half full. In addition, there was about 12 million barrels of Iraqi oil already in the pipeline even before the flow is restored.
